Title: SkillAttack: Automated Red Teaming of Agent Skills through Attack Path Refinement
Abstract: WARNING: THIS PAPER CONTAINS RED-TEAMING RELATED CONTENT.LLM-based agent systems increasingly rely on openregistry skills, which are difficult to vet and expose agents to greater attack risks.These attacks mainly take two forms.Malicious injection attacks embed explicit harmful instructions into skills and are readily caught by auditing.Direct vulnerability attacks target latent flaws in non-malicious skills; however, directly crafted attack prompts often lead to unstable or unverified outcomes.We introduce Skil-lAttack, an automated red-teaming framework that systematically explores executable attack paths from latent vulnerabilities without modifying skill files.Evaluated across 11 target LLMs, SkillAttack substantially outperforms baselines, showing that well-intended skills can pose serious risks in realistic agent interactions.Our evaluation also yields trajectory-level attack traces with verified risk labels, providing a foundation for defense.We also release Skill-RiskBench, a benchmark for skill risk analysis, and train a lightweight pre-execution risk guard that predicts risky invocations from the user request and skill file.The guard outperforms frontier LLM judges and existing safety guard models, highlighting the value of trajectory-grounded supervision for proactive skill defense.
Major_Contribution_Result: SkillAttack is an automated red-teaming loop that finds executable attack paths against latent vulnerabilities in non-malicious agent skills without modifying skill files, evaluated across 11 target LLMs. On Obvious Injections it reports ASRs above 0.73 (up to 0.93) versus Skill-Inject at most 0.40 and Direct Attack near zero; on Contextual Injections ASR reaches 0.85 versus Skill-Inject ≤0.20; on Hot200 real-world skills ASR is up to 0.25. The resulting traces yield SkillRiskBench and a pre-execution risk guard (best Llama-3.1-8B: 0.770 accuracy / 0.769 macro-F1 versus near-chance frontier/safety judges).
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Large-scale ASR evaluation relies on an automated judge that may inherit model-specific biases despite requiring execution evidence. Datasets and guard evaluation are limited to OpenClaw, SKILL-INJECT, and ClawHub Hot200 skill settings; broader registries, harnesses, and deployments remain future work.
Critics: The contribution targets open skill registries and pre-execution risk prediction with trajectory-grounded labels, which is a distinct surface from classic user-prompt IPI. ASR depends on the authors' judge and skill corpora, so absolute numbers should not be generalized beyond those harnesses. Useful for skill-facing agent security evaluation; does not experimentally claim dominance over unrelated agent defenses.
